body.heading: Light without a flame
paragraphs: Most light you know comes with heat: the Sun, a candle, an old-style bulb all glow because they are hot. A glow stick does something rarer — chemiluminescence, light produced directly by a chemical reaction, with almost no heat at all. The reaction's energy is handed to a dye, and the dye sheds the energy as light of a particular colour.

Inside the plastic tube are two liquids kept apart. The outer tube holds an oxalate compound dissolved with the coloured dye; sealed inside that, in a fragile glass vial, is hydrogen peroxide — the same mild bleach sold in pharmacies, here in a stronger supporting role.

body.heading: Bend, snap, shake, glow
paragraphs: Bending the stick snaps the glass vial, and the two liquids mix. The peroxide reacts with the oxalate compound, forming a short-lived, energy-rich intermediate. That intermediate cannot hold its energy, so it passes it to the dye molecules floating nearby — and each dye molecule, settling back down, releases the energy as a photon of light. Choose a different dye and you choose a different colour: the chemistry is the same, the paint is not.

Temperature steers the speed. Warm the stick and the reaction races — brighter light, shorter life. Chill it in a freezer and the reaction crawls, so a spent-looking stick can be coaxed into glowing faintly for hours longer. Either way, once the ingredients are used up, the light ends for good: a glow stick cannot be recharged.

body.heading: Cold light at work
paragraphs: Because they need no batteries, sparks or wiring, glow sticks are standard emergency kit: safe around fuel and water, and happy to work in the rain. Divers carry them, soldiers use them as markers, and deep-sea fishing boats dangle them as lures in the dark water.

Nature invented the trick first. Fireflies and many deep-ocean animals run their own chemiluminescent reactions — the same strategy of turning reaction energy straight into light, refined by evolution long before it was packed in plastic.
